## Goal

Notebook 02 showed that MIIC gives exactly the authors' network when it is run on the authors' three input files. Here we
build those input files ourselves, from the public data, by following the [CausalCCC
tutorial](https://miic.curie.fr/tutorial_causalCCC.php) with its **default parameters**, then run MIIC with the
settings of the authors' server job and compare the network with theirs and with the statements of the paper
(`docs/case_study1_article_description.txt`).

**Inputs:** the NicheNet Seurat object (`data/case1/nichenet_seurat/`), and the authors' server job
(`data/case1/causalccc_server_eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC/`) for its L-R pairs and for the comparison.
**Outputs** in `results/case1/03_tutorial_default_params/`: the CausalCCC input files (`causalccc_files/`, the files
the web server accepts), the MI tables (`MI_tables/`), the MIIC result (`miic_input/`), and two files reused by notebook
04 (`t_cells.rds`, `gene_aliases.tsv`).

::: {.callout-note}
## Running time
The gene selection takes about 10 minutes per cell type and MIIC about 15 to 30 minutes. Both results are saved the
first time and reloaded afterwards. To force a new run, delete `selected_genes.rds` or `miic_input/miic_result.rds`.
:::

## Setup

`miic` must be loaded before `causalCCC`: the gene selection calls `miic()` without importing it. The shared helper
functions are in `scripts/helpers.R` (all case studies) and `scripts/case1/case1_helpers.R` (this notebook and the
next one).

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(Seurat)
library(miic)
library(causalCCC)

find_repo_root <- function(dir = getwd()) {
  while (!(file.exists(file.path(dir, "README.md")) && dir.exists(file.path(dir, "notebooks")))) {
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (parent == dir) stop("Repository root not found. Open the repository folder in Positron.")
    dir <- parent
  }
  dir
}

root        <- find_repo_root()
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "case1", "case1_helpers.R"))

authors_dir <- file.path(root, "data", "case1", "causalccc_server_eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC")
results_dir <- file.path(root, "results", "case1", "03_tutorial_default_params")
dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

**Fix for SeuratObject 5.** `causalCCC.MIselection()` and `causalCCC.mosaic()` read the counts with
`GetAssayData(slot = "counts")`. Since SeuratObject 5.3 the `slot` argument is an error (it was replaced by `layer`).
`patch_causalccc()` makes copies of the two functions with `layer` instead, for this R session only.

```{r}
#| label: patch

patch_causalccc()
```

## 1. The cells

The Seurat object was made with Seurat v3 in 2019, so it is updated first. We keep the CD4⁺ T cells (senders) and
the CD8⁺ T cells (receivers), from both conditions (steady state and 72 h after LCMV infection), as the authors did.

```{r}
#| label: cells
#| warning: false

seurat_obj <- UpdateSeuratObject(readRDS(file.path(root, "data", "case1", "nichenet_seurat", "seuratObj.rds")))
t_cells    <- subset(seurat_obj, subset = celltype %in% c(senders, receivers))
rm(seurat_obj)

table(t_cells$celltype, t_cells$aggregate)   # SS = steady state, LCMV = after infection

saveRDS(t_cells, file.path(results_dir, "t_cells.rds"))
```

**Same counts as the authors?** For each of the 144 variables of the authors' input, we look for the gene of our
object whose counts, in the cells of the same type, are exactly the authors' values (compared as sorted values,
because the authors' table has no cell names).

```{r}
#| label: match-counts

matched <- match_authors_genes(t_cells, authors_dir)

matched |>
  count(found_with = case_when(is.na(object_gene)   ~ "no gene with these counts",
                               object_gene == gene  ~ "same name",
                               .default             = "another name"))

# The genes found under another name
renamed <- matched |> filter(object_gene != gene) |> distinct(authors_name = gene, object_name = object_gene)
renamed

write_tsv(renamed, file.path(results_dir, "gene_aliases.tsv"))
aliases <- setNames(renamed$authors_name, renamed$object_name)   # our name = authors' name
```

Every variable of the authors' input is found in our cells with identical counts. Four genes (seven variables, as some
are measured on both sides) carry a different name in the authors' table, because their count matrix used a newer gene
annotation (for example, Rack1 is the current name of Gnb2l1). From now on we translate our names into theirs when
comparing.

## 2. The ligand–receptor pairs

Case study 1 uses L-R pairs inferred by NicheNet. We take the authors' 18 pairs from their server job and remove the
`_senders` / `_receivers` suffixes; `causalCCC.mosaic()` adds them again where needed. (The tutorial's own function
for L-R pairs, `causalCCC.links()`, uses LIANA and currently fails for mouse data inside OmnipathR.)

```{r}
#| label: lr-pairs

interact_edges <- read_tsv(file.path(authors_dir, "clean_interact_edges.tsv"),
                           col_names = c("ligands", "receptors"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), strip_suffix)) |>
  distinct()

interact_edges
```

## 3. Build the CausalCCC input with the default parameters

`build_causalccc_input()` (in `scripts/case1/case1_helpers.R`) runs the tutorial steps:

1. `causalCCC.MIselection()`: for each cell type, the genes sharing the most mutual information (MI) with the ligands
   (CD4⁺) or with the receptors (CD8⁺). With the default `n_genes`, it keeps 4 genes per gene of interest, i.e. 40 for
   the 10 ligands and 32 for the 8 receptors, plus the 3 best genes of each gene of interest;
2. `causalCCC.mosaic()`: the mosaic table, one row per cell, `NA` outside each cell type's genes;
3. `causalCCC.state_order()` and `causalCCC.layout()`: the variable descriptions and the drawing layout.

```{r}
#| label: build
#| message: false
#| results: hide

default_settings <- list(remove_ribo = FALSE, n_genes = NULL, sender_genes_in_receivers = FALSE)
built <- build_causalccc_input(t_cells, interact_edges, default_settings, results_dir)

```

Number of variables of each group in the new input:

```{r}
#| label: groups

count(built$state_order, group)
```

The genes ranked by MI with the genes of interest, as drawn by `causalCCC.MIselection()`:

```{r}
#| label: heatmaps
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: 100%

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(results_dir, "MI_tables", paste0(c(senders, receivers), "_MI_heatmap_filtered.png")))
```

## 4. Run MIIC with the authors' settings

The four files in `causalccc_files/` can be uploaded to the web server. Instead, we run MIIC locally with
`scripts/run_miic.R`, which uses the settings of the authors' server job (notebook 02, section 2), in particular the
confidence filter (100 shuffles, ratio 0.01) and the strict orientation threshold (0.01). The server's default settings
are different, so a network from the server with its default settings could not be compared fairly with the authors'.

```{r}
#| label: miic

miic_result <- run_miic_authors_settings(built, results_dir, root)
attr(miic_result, "run_time")
```

## 5. Compare with the authors

We read both networks in the same format: one node per gene and side (`B2m(S)` in sender cells, `B2m(R)` in receiver
cells), our gene names translated into the authors'. The authors' network is the one of their January 2025 run
(`edgesList.miic.summary.txt_save`, notebook 02).

```{r}
#| label: read-networks

authors_nodes <- read_nodes(read_tsv(file.path(authors_dir, "clean_state_order.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE))
authors_net   <- read_network(read_tsv(file.path(authors_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt_save"),
                                       show_col_types = FALSE), authors_nodes)

our_nodes <- read_nodes(built$state_order, aliases)
our_net   <- read_network(miic_result$all.edges.summary, our_nodes)
```

**Genes.**

```{r}
#| label: compare-genes

bind_rows(authors = summarise_nodes(authors_nodes, authors_nodes),
          ours    = summarise_nodes(our_nodes, authors_nodes), .id = "network")

# The authors' genes missing from our input
setdiff(authors_nodes$node, our_nodes$node) |> sort()
```

**Links.**

```{r}
#| label: compare-links

compare_networks(our_net, authors_net)
```

## 6. The links described in the paper

The paper describes 17 links of Figure 2 (`paper_links` in `case1_helpers.R`). For each, the table gives its
orientation in each network, or "absent".

```{r}
#| label: paper-links

check_paper_links(list(authors = authors_net, ours = our_net)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## What we learned

**The data are the authors'.** Our CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells (2,562 and 1,645, both conditions pooled) have exactly the
counts of the authors' input, for all 144 variables; four genes only carry newer names in their table.

**The tutorial with default parameters does not reproduce the authors' input.** It selects 112 genes (60 sender, 52
receiver), of which only 61 are among the authors' 144, and 33 are ribosomal protein genes, none of which the authors
kept.

**Hence a different network.** With the authors' MIIC settings, our network has 282 links and contains 107 of the
authors' 364 (92 with the same orientation). Of the 17 links described in the paper, 12 are found. Three of the 5 missing
ones involve receiver genes that the default selection does not keep (Cd8b1, Ly6c1); the other two (H2-K1 – Shisa5,
H2-D1 – Mir703) are between genes present in our input, so the other selected genes changed the network around them. The central statement, Stat1 →
B2m as a genuine cause, holds. Stat1 – Isg20 is oriented Stat1 → Isg20 here, bidirected in the authors' network.

Since MIIC is reproducible (notebook 02), these differences come from the gene selection. Notebook 04 looks for the
settings that explain them.
